analysis.one_liner: Repeals the estate tax rule that stopped wealthy families from freezing the taxable value of their businesses before passing them to heirs.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the estate tax's anti-valuation-freeze rule was introduced with 28 senators backing it, got a Finance Committee hearing in May 1989, and never received a vote before the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have wiped out section 2036(c) of the tax code, a rule adopted in 1987 to stop a technique called an "estate freeze." In a freeze, a family head keeps the low-risk, low-growth part of a business (like preferred stock) while giving the fast-growing part to the children, so the taxable estate stays small. The 1987 rule taxed that arrangement more aggressively. Repealing it would have restored the ability of wealthy owners of family businesses to pass on large amounts of wealth with little estate tax. The bill had 27 cosponsors from both parties, but after one hearing it went nowhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Wealthy owners of family businesses and other large estates, who could once again use "estate freeze" arrangements: the older generation keeps preferred (low-growth) stock while the children take the fast-appreciating common stock, capping the taxable value of the estate. Estate tax planners and advisers to these families would also gain business.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wealthy family-business owners and large estates

how_it_helps.text: The bill repealed section 2036(c), a 1987 rule that forced wealthy families to include the value of certain 'freeze' transfers in the taxable estate of the person who retained control of the assets.

The CRS summary describes the bill as repealing estate tax provisions that brought 'certain types of transfers with a retained life estate' into the gross estate — that is, the rule that stopped a family head from locking in a low taxable value by handing growth to heirs while keeping control.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury and ordinary taxpayers, who would make up revenue lost to the estate tax if wealthy families again shrink their taxable estates through freeze techniques. The estate tax generally applies only to the largest estates, but its burden or avoidance patterns affect the broader tax base.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ordinary taxpayers via the estate-tax base

drawbacks.text: Section 2036(c), though overbroad and criticized as unworkable, was the only check at the time on 'estate freeze' arrangements that let wealthy families pass on appreciating businesses at little tax cost. Repealing it without any replacement would have opened the door back to that practice.
The bill was a full repeal with no substitute rule, so even taxpayers and advisers who agreed the provision was badly drawn had no compromise mechanism to consider.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If it had passed, the cost would have fallen on the estate tax's purpose: families could again shift appreciating business assets to heirs while keeping control, shrinking the tax base that applies mostly to large estates. The benefit went only to those wealthy families and their advisers. The bill's repeal was broad — it wiped out the anti-freeze rule entirely rather than fixing its overreach — so there was no narrower middle ground offered here. Its death preserved the rule (later replaced by a different, workable approach), which better served ordinary taxpayers and the estate tax's integrity.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 1989, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which held a hearing in May, and then nothing happened — no vote ever came before the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Senator Daschle introduced the bill on April 19, 1989, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee.
Twenty-seven other senators, split between 14 Democrats and 13 Republicans, signed on as cosponsors — notable bipartisan support for a bill that would relieve wealthy estates of a tax rule.
The Finance Committee held hearings on the bill on May 17, 1989, its only action beyond the referral.
After the hearing, the bill saw no further action: it was never voted on by the committee or either chamber, and died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal estate tax kept a check on estate-freeze arrangements, so the Treasury and ordinary taxpayers who do not use these planning techniques were better off. Wealthy families looking to freeze their estate values gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The estate tax and ordinary taxpayers

for.name: Sen. Thomas Daschle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal section 2036(c) on April 19, 1989.

for.name: 27 Senate cosponsors (14 Democrats, 13 Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the repeal, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship from more than a quarter of the Senate.

for.name: Senate Finance Committee
for.what_they_did: Held hearings on the bill on May 17, 1989, then took no further action and never reported it out for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: Support was genuinely bipartisan — 14 of 55 Senate Democrats and 13 of 45 Senate Republicans cosponsored — and no opposition ever surfaced on the record, because the bill died in committee without a vote.

industries.industry: Estate planners and tax advisers to wealthy families
industries.note: Repealing 2036(c) would have reopened the market for sophisticated estate-freeze planning, but the bill died, so the provision (in some form) stayed in place and advisers continued working within or around the restraints on freeze techniques.

industries.industry: Owners of large family businesses and wealthy estates
industries.note: These are the direct beneficiaries of repeal: the freeze rule made it costly to pass appreciating businesses to the next generation at a low tax value. The bill's failure kept that cost on the books.
